summary.text: Write each divisor as \(2^j o\) with \(o\) dividing the odd part of \(n\); for each such \(o\), exactly one power-of-two multiple lies in the middle interval iff both \(o\) and its complementary odd divisor are below \(\sqrt{2n}\). Since the two complementary odd divisors cannot both exceed \(\sqrt{2n}\), summing this criterion and pairing complements shows that subtracting the middle-divisor count leaves two equal copies of the above-threshold count.

full_proof.text:
Let \(n\ge 1\). We write
\[
n=2^K m,
\]
where \(K\ge 0\) and \(m\) is odd. Thus \(m\) is the odd part of \(n\).

Let
\[
O(n)=\#\{d:d\mid n,\ d\text{ odd}\}
\]
and let
\[
M(n)=\#\{d:d\mid n,\ \sqrt{n/2}\le d<\sqrt{2n}\}.
\]
The latter are precisely the middle divisors of \(n\). Since all quantities are nonnegative, their defining inequalities may equivalently be written without square roots as
\[
n\le 2d^2\quad\text{and}\quad d^2<2n.
\]
By definition, the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=O(n)-M(n).
\]
We prove that
\[
a(n)=2\#\{d:d\mid n,\ d\text{ odd},\ d>\sqrt{2n}\}.
\]
Equivalently, the final inequality can be written \(2n<d^2\).

First observe that the odd divisors of \(n\) are exactly the divisors of \(m\). Indeed, every divisor of the odd number \(m\) is an odd divisor of \(n=2^K m\). Conversely, if an odd number divides \(2^K m\), it is relatively prime to \(2^K\), so it must divide \(m\). Consequently,
\[
O(n)=\tau(m),
\]
where \(\tau(m)\) denotes the number of positive divisors of \(m\).

We next count the middle divisors by grouping all divisors of \(n\) according to their odd part. Every positive divisor \(d\) of \(n\) has a unique expression
\[
d=2^j o,
\]
where \(0\le j\le K\) and \(o\mid m\). Here \(o\) is odd and is the odd part of \(d\). Conversely, every number \(2^j o\) with \(0\le j\le K\) and \(o\mid m\) divides \(n\).

Fix a divisor \(o\) of \(m\), and put
\[
q=\frac{m}{o}.
\]
Thus \(o,q\) are positive odd integers and \(oq=m\). The divisors of \(n\) whose odd part is \(o\) are exactly
\[
x_j=2^j o\qquad(0\le j\le K).
\]
We claim that exactly one of these is a middle divisor if
\[
o^2<2n\quad\text{and}\quad q^2<2n,
\]
and none of them is a middle divisor otherwise.

To prove this claim, set
\[
L=\sqrt{n/2},\qquad U=\sqrt{2n}.
\]
Notice that \(U=2L\). The sequence \(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_K\) doubles at every step. Therefore at most one term can lie in the half-open interval \([L,U)\): if \(x_i\ge L\), then every later term, beginning with \(x_{i+1}=2x_i\), is at least \(2L=U\).

There is a term in \([L,U)\) exactly when the initial term is below the upper endpoint and the final term reaches the lower endpoint, that is, exactly when
\[
x_0<U\quad\text{and}\quad x_K\ge L.
\]
Indeed, necessity is immediate because the sequence is increasing. Conversely, assume these two endpoint conditions and choose the least \(j\) such that \(x_j\ge L\). If \(j=0\), then \(x_j=x_0<U\). If \(j>0\), minimality gives \(x_{j-1}<L\), and hence
\[
x_j=2x_{j-1}<2L=U.
\]
Thus in either case \(L\le x_j<U\), proving existence. The preceding doubling argument proves uniqueness.

The first endpoint condition is simply
\[
x_0<U\iff o<\sqrt{2n}\iff o^2<2n.
\]
It remains to translate the second endpoint condition. Since \(x_K=2^K o\), we have
\[
x_K\ge L
\iff n\le 2(2^K o)^2.
\]
Using \(n=2^K m=2^Koq\) and cancelling the positive factor \(2^K o\), this becomes
\[
q\le 2^{K+1}o.
\]
The number \(q\) is odd, whereas \(2^{K+1}o\) is even, so equality is impossible. Thus this is equivalent to
\[
q<2^{K+1}o.
\]
On the other hand, again using \(n=2^Koq\) and cancelling the positive factor \(q\),
\[
q^2<2n
\iff q^2<2^{K+1}oq
\iff q<2^{K+1}o.
\]
Hence \(x_K\ge L\) is equivalent to \(q^2<2n\), as required. This proves the claim about each odd-part fiber.

For a statement \(P\), write \(\mathbf 1_P\) for \(1\) when \(P\) is true and \(0\) otherwise. Summing the fiber count over all divisors \(o\) of \(m\), we obtain
\[
M(n)=\sum_{o\mid m}
 \mathbf 1_{\,o^2<2n\ \text{and}\ (m/o)^2<2n}.
\]

We now rewrite each summand. Fix \(o\mid m\) and again put \(q=m/o\). Both \(o\) and \(q\) are odd. Therefore neither \(o^2\) nor \(q^2\) can equal \(2n\), because an odd square is odd while \(2n\) is even. Thus each of \(o^2,q^2\) is either strictly less than or strictly greater than \(2n\).

Moreover, they cannot both be greater than \(2n\). If they were, then multiplication would give
\[
(o q)^2>4n^2.
\]
But \(oq=m\), and \(m\le n\), so
\[
(oq)^2=m^2\le n^2,
\]
a contradiction. Consequently, among the two conditions \(o^2>2n\) and \(q^2>2n\), at most one can hold. It follows by considering the three possible cases—both squares below \(2n\), only \(o^2\) above, or only \(q^2\) above—that
\[
\mathbf 1_{\,o^2<2n\ \text{and}\ q^2<2n}
=1-\mathbf 1_{\,2n<o^2}-\mathbf 1_{\,2n<q^2}.
\]
Indeed, when both squares are below \(2n\), both sides equal \(1\); when exactly one is above \(2n\), both sides equal \(0\). The excluded fourth case, in which both are above, cannot occur.

Substituting this identity into the sum for \(M(n)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
M(n)
&=\sum_{o\mid m}1
 -\sum_{o\mid m}\mathbf 1_{\,2n<o^2}
 -\sum_{o\mid m}\mathbf 1_{\,2n<(m/o)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The map
\[
o\longmapsto \frac{m}{o}
\]
is an involution, and hence a bijection, on the positive divisors of \(m\). Therefore the final two sums are equal. Define
\[
H(n)=\#\{o:o\mid m,\ 2n<o^2\}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{o\mid m}1=\tau(m)=O(n),
\]
and each of the other two sums equals \(H(n)\). Hence
\[
M(n)=O(n)-2H(n).
\]
Rearranging,
\[
a(n)=O(n)-M(n)=2H(n).
\]
Finally, divisors of \(m\) are exactly the odd divisors of \(n\), and for a positive integer \(o\),
\[
2n<o^2\iff o>\sqrt{2n}.
\]
Thus \(H(n)\) is exactly the number of odd divisors of \(n\) greater than \(\sqrt{2n}\). We conclude that for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\boxed{a(n)=2\#\{d:d\mid n,\ d\text{ odd},\ d>\sqrt{2n}\}}.
\]
